title: Beijing Restaurant Serves Food Fit for Emperors
paragraphs: For centuries, the food served to China's emperors was surrounded by strict rules and elaborate rituals. Although China's last imperial dynasty, the Qing, came to an end more than a hundred years ago, a restaurant in Beijing is keeping this remarkable culinary tradition alive.

Fangshan Restaurant was founded in 1925 by former chefs of the Qing court in Beihai Park, a garden where members of the royal family once rested, handled government affairs and performed ritual sacrifices. According to the restaurant's assistant general manager, Di Xin, its name means "imitating the imperial cuisine." The restaurant's executive chef, Fan Liangliang, explained that its cooking combines the traditions of the Manchu people, who ruled during the Qing Dynasty, with those of the Han, China's majority ethnic group.

The restaurant's most popular items are pea flour cake and red bean rolls, and during the busy season, customers order more than 200 cakes a day. Another famous treat is the so-called "dream pastry." According to Zhou Tong, a chef at the restaurant, Empress Dowager Cixi once dreamed about a pastry, and the very next morning, the same treat was served at her breakfast. She was so delighted that she rewarded the chef with a silver ingot. The pastry was originally called "minced pork pancake," but it has since become known as "dream pastry."

Imperial cooking is extremely labor-intensive. Everything is done by hand, and blenders and food processors are not allowed. Beans are crushed using sieves, and certain flours are prepared in specially made copper pots. As Zhou put it, a machine may be more convenient, but the texture is completely different. Chefs also use a technique called "nizihuo," in which fish, shrimp or chicken is minced into a smooth paste and shaped into decorative forms, such as frogs, birds and flowers.

Dining in the imperial court was also full of ceremony. According to Teng Deyong, a researcher at the Palace Museum, drinking milk tea was an important first step at Qing banquets. The emperor would offer wine or food to princes and officials, who had to perform rites to pay their respects before they could eat or drink.
Staff at Fangshan tell customers the stories behind the dishes, and as Fan said, diners experience the weight of history.
